newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK banks mostly positive on forex business - survey.
newsitem.headline: HK banks mostly positive on forex business - survey.

text.p: A survey of Hong Kong bank treasury departments found that most executives foresee their business remaining steady or improving in coming years.
The outlook would be better if China's currency becomes fully convertible, but most did not expect Hong Kong's handover to China by itself to have a significant impact on business.
The survey of 130 treasury executives was taken by the Hong Kong Financial Markets Association.

The survey found that 41 percent expected their treasury activities to remain unchanged in the next three years, while 43 percent said they foresee expansion, particularly in regional currencies, derivatives and treasury marketing.
Sixteen percent expected business to contract, especially in foreign exchange trading.
Most respondents said they believed that regional currencies would be the focus of future expansion, followed by high value structured transactions and Group of 10 currency trading.
Hong Kong's traditional focus on Group of 10 currencies has modest growth potential, with the advent of a single European currency expected to limit volatility and trading opportunities.

Andrew Fung, head of capital markets at Commonwealth Bank of Australia and the Financial Markets Association chairman, acknowledged that Singapore has an edge in interbank trading of Asian currencies.
But he said the large pool of fund managers and private investors in Hong Kong means that local banks can prosper by offering high-value, customer-driven structured products.
"It is true that business is contracting, but only in interbank dealing. Banks here are now moving to second generation products, like options and derivatives, he said.
Hong Kong was ranked fifth in the world last year in terms of foreign exchange trade, with average daily turnover of US$91 billion. Singapore was fourth, with US$105 billion in turnover.

Eight-eight percent of those surveyed foresee a significant expansion in treasury business in Hong Kong if China's currency becomes fully convertible. The remaining 12 percent did not expect any significant change in that event.
Beijing plans to allow full convertibility of the renminbi on the capital account in the future, but no timetable has been set. The renminbi is convertible on the current account.

Eighty-two percent of respondents forecast better business if China's commercial banks are permitted to participate in renminbi non-deliverable forward transactions, while 18 percent do not expect an expansion in business under that scenario.
At present, only offshore entities can deal in non-deliverable forward transactions, which are used to hedge currencies that are not fully convertible, such as the renminbi and the Korean won.

Sixty-six percent of the respondents said they did not expect Hong Kong's handover to China to cause any significant changes in their treasury business, while 32 percent forecast a change for the better and two percent were negative.
Fung said the organisation has been actively lobbying China to funnel more treasury management business toward Hong Kong.
"The decision of the Peoples Bank of China to set up a branch in Hong Kong to manage part of its reserves is good news," said Fung. China has more than US$110 billion in foreign currency reserves.

Respondents said Hong Kong's future as a financial centre would be determined by its prosperity, investor confidence, the stability of the financial system and the threat posed by Asian competitors, such as Singapore.
